title: Latent Heat and Change of State

blocks.text: Put a thermometer in a pot of water on a hot stove and watch it climb steadily to 100 °C — then stop dead. The gas is still roaring and energy is still pouring in, but the reading refuses to budge until the last drop has boiled away. Where is all that energy going?

blocks.markdown:
It is going into **separating the molecules**, not into speeding them up. Heat that produces a change of state without any change in temperature is called **latent heat** — from the Latin for *hidden*, because a thermometer cannot detect it.

During melting or boiling, the energy supplied does work against the forces of attraction between molecules. Average molecular kinetic energy — and therefore temperature — stays constant until the change of state is complete.

blocks.title: Specific latent heat
blocks.text: The specific latent heat of fusion is the quantity of heat required to change 1 kg of a solid into liquid at its melting point without change of temperature. The specific latent heat of vaporisation is the quantity of heat required to change 1 kg of a liquid into vapour at its boiling point without change of temperature. Both are measured in J kg⁻¹.

blocks.markdown:
### Why vaporisation needs so much more energy

Compare $3.36 \times 10^{5}$ with $2.26 \times 10^{6}$ — boiling water needs nearly **seven times** as much energy per kilogram as melting ice. Two reasons:

1. In melting, molecules only need enough energy to slip past one another; in vaporisation they must be pulled **completely free** of each other.
2. The vapour occupies a far greater volume, so work must also be done pushing back the atmosphere.

blocks.title: Melting a block of ice
blocks.prompt: Calculate the heat required to melt 0.50 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 0 °C. Take the specific latent heat of fusion of ice as 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.

steps.text: There is no temperature change, so use the latent heat formula rather than Q = mcΔθ.
Substitute the mass and the specific latent heat of fusion.
State the answer with its unit.

blocks.title: A two-stage heating problem
blocks.prompt: Calculate the total heat required to convert 2.0 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 100 °C. Take l_f = 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹ and c_water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

steps.text: Break the problem into stages. Stage 1: melt the ice at 0 °C using latent heat.
Stage 2: raise the resulting water from 0 °C to 100 °C using specific heat capacity.

blocks.markdown:
### Reading a heating or cooling curve

On a graph of temperature against time for a substance heated steadily:

- **Sloping sections** mean the temperature is rising, so $Q = mc\,\Delta\theta$ applies and only one state is present.
- **Horizontal (flat) sections** mean a change of state is happening. The temperature is constant, so $Q = ml$ applies and both states coexist.

The flat section at the boiling point is always much longer than the one at the melting point, exactly as the latent heat values predict.

blocks.title: Why steam scalds worse than boiling water
blocks.text: Steam at 100 °C and water at 100 °C are at the same temperature, but when steam condenses on your skin it releases 2.26 × 10⁶ J for every kilogram — its latent heat of vaporisation — before it even begins to cool. That is why a steam burn is far more severe than a splash of boiling water.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: Never put a Δθ into a latent heat term and never leave l out of a change-of-state stage. Sketch the temperature-time path first, mark each stage, and decide for each one whether it is mcΔθ or ml. Multi-stage questions are marked stage by stage, so a clear layout earns marks even if one arithmetic step slips.

points: Latent heat is the heat absorbed or released during a change of state with no change of temperature.
Q = ml, where l is the specific latent heat in J kg⁻¹ — there is no Δθ term.
During melting or boiling the energy separates molecules instead of increasing their kinetic energy, so temperature stays constant.
For water, l_f = 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹ and l_v = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; vaporisation needs far more because molecules must be fully separated.
In a multi-stage problem, use mcΔθ for the sloping stages and ml for the flat ones, then add.
